title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite and packed with stars, why isn't the entire night sky ablaze with light?
summary: A simple observation — that the night sky is dark rather than uniformly bright — turns out to be a genuine clue about the size, age, and structure of the universe.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and look up. Between the stars, the sky is black. This seems too obvious to need explaining, but in the 1820s the astronomer Heinrich Olbers realized it was actually a serious problem. If the universe is infinite, eternal, and roughly uniformly filled with stars, then every line of sight from Earth should eventually terminate on the surface of some star. The whole sky should be a wall of light, roughly as bright as the sun. It isn't. Why not?

The Logic of the Paradox

The argument is deceptively simple. A star at distance d looks dimmer by a factor of 1/d² — farther stars are fainter. But in a uniform infinite universe, the number of stars in a thin shell at distance d grows with the shell's surface area, which scales as d². These two effects exactly cancel: each shell of stars, no matter how far away, contributes the same total amount of light to the sky. Add up infinitely many shells and you get infinite brightness. Even accounting for stars blocking each other, every point in the sky should eventually be covered by some stellar surface, making the whole sky as bright as an average star.

Wrong Turns Along the Way

Early proposed solutions were plausible but wrong. Maybe interstellar dust absorbs the extra light? No — over infinite time, dust would absorb energy until it glowed as hot as the stars themselves, radiating the light right back out. The paradox survives naive fixes because it's really an argument about the geometry of an infinite, static, eternal universe — and that assumption is what turns out to be false.

The Real Resolution Is About Time, Not Just Space

The universe is not eternal and static; it had a beginning roughly 13.8 billion years ago, and light travels at a finite speed. That means we can only ever see stars whose light has had time to reach us — a finite observable volume, not an infinite one. Beyond a certain distance, there simply hasn't been enough cosmic history for their light to arrive yet. Compounding this, the universe is expanding, so light from very distant, very early sources gets redshifted into infrared and radio wavelengths we can't see with our eyes, and the energy density of that light is diluted by the expansion itself. Stars also don't live forever; a truly infinite universe of eternal stars was never physically realistic to begin with.

What the Darkness Tells Us

So the darkness of the night sky is not a trivial fact — it's indirect observational evidence that the universe had a finite beginning and is expanding. Olbers never solved his own paradox, but posing it clearly was itself the achievement: it showed that "the universe is infinite and static" makes a testable, falsifiable prediction, and that prediction fails. Few naked-eye observations carry that much cosmological weight.

perspectives.title: Astrophysics Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite speed of light means we see a finite observable universe. The night sky is dark because most of the universe is causally out of view — its light literally hasn't arrived yet.

perspectives.title: Cosmological Perspective
perspectives.description: Expansion redshifts ancient starlight out of the visible spectrum and dilutes its energy density. A static universe would look very different from the one we actually inhabit.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers wasn't the first to notice the puzzle, but his clear formulation made it a genuine scientific problem rather than a curiosity, decades before the Big Bang model existed to resolve it.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is a rare case of a mundane, universally available observation forcing a strong conclusion about the structure of the entire cosmos — a reminder that big theories can hinge on small facts.
